story.title: THE ROAD THAT CUT A COUNTRY THIN AS PAPER
story.deck: The only road out of a flooding valley runs through a country as thin as paper, whose people have only ever met humans as sudden walls. Illuminara cannot perceive their plane, so she asks its speaker what a whole person would look like, and lies down across the road to show her.
story.shape: Seven scenes across eleven days: a cold line on a road, a conversation in frost, a governor's one night, a body read slice by slice, a calendar proved on an empty truck, the arithmetic of nine days, and the last crossing.

scenes.title: The Cold Line
paragraphs: *Orrin Cut, kilometre 14 · twelve days before the crest, 05:40*

The road ran through the Cut like thread through a needle, and halfway along it the air changed. Illuminara felt it before she saw the survey flags: a line of cold across the tarmac, straight as a ruled edge. Fog on the upslope side stopped at it. On the downslope side the dawn was only dawn.

Four road crew had walked into it since the autumn rains. One had lost feeling down his left side for a week. A gauge nailed to a post read minus six on the line and eleven above zero a pace either way.
Ilse Brandvold, the survey lead, had slept in her truck. She pointed at a steel plate bolted flat to the road, a metre square, white with rime.

**Ilse**  
Six weeks of geophone logs. Every ninety minutes it pulls back for fourteen minutes, then comes down again. I thought it was groundwater. Then I put the plate on the line to measure the frost, and the frost wrote back.
Marks were forming on the rime as they watched, thin and deliberate, as if someone were breathing them there.

**Ilse**  
I have eleven hundred of those. I understand perhaps forty. The speaker is called Vesh. It's a country, Illuminara. A sheet no thicker than a coin, and the Cut goes straight through the middle of it.

**Illuminara**  
And the governor?

**Ilse**  
Opens the road at noon. Nine thousand buses and trucks, six days, no stopping. The river crests in twelve. I can't put a country on his desk. I have a steel plate and a cold spot.

Illuminara crouched and laid her palm on the rime. It burned, and under the burn she felt something she had no word for, like being looked at from the side. *I can hold a lane open,* she thought. *The lane is not the problem. I can't perceive what she can't show him, and I won't pretend to.*

scenes.title: What the Frost Said
paragraphs: *The plate on the line · twelve days before the crest, 07:10*
Vesh's words came a few strokes at a time. Ilse read them out in her flat survey voice, and Illuminara answered to the plate itself, because it seemed rude to answer to anyone else.

**Vesh**  
You are weather to us. A wall rises where there was a street, grows, narrows, is gone. Nothing is behind it. Ninety-three of us have stood inside the rising. Eleven streets are cut in two and do not rejoin.

**Illuminara**  
I'm sorry. I'm also here to ask something of you, and I would rather you heard it from me than discovered it. Nine thousand vehicles must pass in twelve days, or two hundred thousand people are under the river. I don't yet know how to pass them without cutting more of you.

**Vesh**  
You ask patience of a people whose houses you halve with every wheel. Tell me when I am allowed to be afraid.
Illuminara did not answer at once. *A reasonable question,* she thought. *A true one.*

**Illuminara**  
Now. You're allowed now. Tell me exactly what you're afraid of, so I stop guessing.

**Vesh**  
That we are not seen. A blade has no one behind it. We have never met one of you. We have met the parts of you the road lets through.

It landed in her slowly. To Sheaf a person was not a person at all. A foot was a ring that appeared, swelled and shrank. A bus was a wall. No one in that country had ever watched a thing for long enough to call it a thing.

**Illuminara**  
What would a whole one look like to you?

**Vesh**  
Slow. A shape that stays long enough to be a shape, then another a little changed. We would read it as we read a coast.
*A coast, taken one slice at a time,* she thought, and offered the only thing she had that was not a request.

**Illuminara**  
I can lie across the road and pass through the line as slowly as you choose. You set the speed. You say stop, and I stop.
The frost took a long time to answer.

**Vesh**  
It is a danger to you. It would be a danger to us if you were wrong. Come in our sleep quarter, when the streets are empty. Come with no machine.

scenes.title: One Night
paragraphs: *Staging yard, Haldane Junction · twelve days before the crest, 11:20*

Governor Halloran Ashe stood at a map of the river with a pencil behind his ear and a driver's funeral card in his breast pocket. He had buried the man on Tuesday. He heard Ilse's whole report without once looking at his watch, which Illuminara noticed and respected.

**Governor Ashe**  
I believe you. I believe there's a country in my road. I also have two hundred thousand people between a river and a hill, and a convoy that can't idle. What do you want?

**Illuminara**  
One night and the morning after. Hold the convoy here. I'm not asking you to close the road. I'm asking for a way to run it that doesn't cut anyone.

**Governor Ashe**  
That costs days. I had six. The crest is twelve.

**Illuminara**  
It may cost three. It won't cost twelve. If I can't show you something by noon tomorrow, open it. The order is yours, not mine.

**Governor Ashe**  
And if what you show me is a creature's feelings against my people's lives?

**Illuminara**  
Then I won't stand in the road. But her streets are real, Governor. So are yours.
He took the pencil from behind his ear and wrote *noon* across the staging yard on the map, hard enough to tear the paper.

scenes.title: Slice by Slice
paragraphs: *Orrin Cut, the line · eleven days before the crest, 02:20*

She lay on her back across the centre line in a thin coat, head toward Ilse's lamp, feet toward the downslope dark. Dov Karakas, the night marshal, kept the cones. Ilse knelt at the plate with a notebook on her knee. Nothing electronic was within thirty metres. Vesh had asked for that.

**Vesh**  
A thumb's width in each of your minutes. Begin.

Illuminara dug her heels into the tarmac and slid. The cold met her toes first. It crossed them like a thread drawn tight and climbed her, one band of ice laid against her skin at a time. On the plate the frost began to write, not words now but shapes, small and closed.

**Vesh**  
A ring. It grows. Another beside it. They are joining.

**Illuminara**  
My ankles. Then a leg. Then the other.

**Vesh**  
Why does it not vanish?

**Illuminara**  
Because I'm staying.

She slid on. Her knees made two long ovals, her hips one wide one, and at the ribs a curve that swelled and fell, swelled and fell. Ilse read it out in a whisper, and Illuminara felt the line of cold cross her chest like a hand laid flat.

**Vesh**  
It moves in a rhythm. Is it failing?

**Illuminara**  
Breathing. It means I'm alive.

The shape stopped changing for a long time. Illuminara lay with the cold across her ribs and her teeth beginning to chatter, and understood with a clarity that surprised her that she was being read. A country was walking the length of her, one lamp-lit street at a time, and for the first time learning that the wall had edges.
Then Vesh asked for the hand. She lifted it a thumb's width at a time, and the frost divided the curve into five, small and astonished.

**Vesh**  
You are not a blade. You are long. You have parts.

**Illuminara**  
So do you, I think.

The cold crossed her hair at 03:46. The frost drew a last round shape, and the whole of her was a drawing. At 03:49 the line melted off the plate and off the road all at once, the way a held breath is let go.

**Vesh**  
The market is closing. The streets are empty. Look.

The frost drew it for them: lanes of lamps going dark in order, doors shutting, a square emptying like a bath. Fourteen minutes of nothing. Illuminara, who had never been shown a country's evening, lay on wet tarmac and watched it breathe.

scenes.title: The Calendar
paragraphs: *The line · eleven days before the crest, 05:12*
Ilse had a sealed envelope in her breast pocket. She had written it at nine the previous evening from six weeks of geophone logs and nothing Vesh had told her, and had given it to Dov to hold.

**Ilse**  
If the logs are a calendar, it goes quiet at five-seventeen for fourteen minutes, give or take three. It's thickest from about six-twenty to six-forty, with the streets full. And the closing you saw at three-forty-nine was two minutes off my card. That's the part I got wrong.

**Dov**  
Two minutes is a good miss.

**Illuminara**  
Why two?
Ilse asked the plate. The frost answered quickly.

**Vesh**  
Our market runs with the river. It lags a little each cycle. Tell your surveyor to keep a table, not a constant.

Ilse wrote *table, not constant* in the margin of her envelope. At 05:18 the line melted off the road, one minute after her card. They sent an empty flatbed across by remote at fifteen kilometres an hour with forty metres of road behind each marker, and Vesh's report was on the plate before the truck cleared the line. *No street cut. A wall passed. Nothing was in it.*
Then the frost came back. It came at 05:29, two minutes early and without warning, a white line creeping across the tarmac from the plate outward.

**Vesh**  
Market reopens. Stop.

**Dov**  
That's a red light I can read.

Dov dropped the gate on a second flatbed in the queue. It halted a metre short of the line, and nobody argued with a strip of frost. Illuminara watched the gate and thought of what the governor needed to hear. *Sheaf can stop us, and does, and we can see it happen.*

At 06:20 the cold gauge fell to minus nine and held. Sheaf's streets filled, Vesh said, as they did every morning when Brass Street opened its stalls. It lifted at 06:41. Ilse's card had said six-twenty to six-forty.

scenes.title: Nine Days
paragraphs: *Staging yard, Haldane Junction · eleven days before the crest, 11:50*
She put the arithmetic on the governor's table because he had asked for arithmetic and nothing else.

**Illuminara**  
Sixteen closings a day. Four fall in Sheaf's sleep quarter, and Vesh asks us not to use them. That leaves twelve pulses of fourteen minutes. One lane, because the second sits over their thickest streets and they refuse it. Forty metres between vehicles at fifteen kilometres an hour is one about every ten seconds, eighty-four a pulse. Twelve pulses is a thousand and eight a day. Nine days is nine thousand and seventy-two.

**Governor Ashe**  
Nine days. I wanted six.

**Illuminara**  
The crest is in eleven. You keep two days in hand, and nobody is cut.
Ashe studied Ilse's table, then the frost photographs Dov had pinned beside it. For a while he said nothing.

**Governor Ashe**  
And the eleven streets already cut? I won't open a road I can be accused of lying about.

**Illuminara**  
Vesh says they knit in seventy days if nothing crosses. After the evacuation the Cut closes to heavy traffic for seventy days, ambulances only, and only in a closing. Sheaf takes a seat on a joint crossing authority. The road is never widened without its consent. The names of the ninety-three go into the authority's charter, in their own script, and are read aloud once a year.

**Governor Ashe**  
Seventy days. My reconstruction trucks.

**Illuminara**  
Will take the river road when the water drops. Longer, I know. Ilse has costed it.

Ashe let out a long breath. Then he took the pencil and, under the order to open the road, wrote the sentence that would govern it. Convoys cross only in a pulse. The marshal follows the frost. A driver who crosses outside a pulse loses his licence for a year.

**Governor Ashe**  
And if one of my drivers decides he's in a hurry?

**Dov**  
Then he meets me at the gate, Governor. And the gate meets him first.

scenes.title: The Ninety-Third Name
paragraphs: *The line · two days before the crest, 03:49*

On the ninth night the last bus crossed in the first pulse after the sleep quarter, a school bus with a cracked mirror and eleven people asleep across the back seats. It went over the line at fifteen kilometres an hour with forty metres of road behind it, and the frost did not stir.
Nobody cheered. Dov lowered the gate, the frost came down over the road like a held cloth, and then Vesh wrote.

**Vesh**  
Nine thousand and sixty-one passed. Nothing in them is cut. We will say so in the square tonight.

Then Vesh wrote the names. Ninety-three, in Sheaf's script, one to a line, and Ilse read them aloud into the dawn as the frost let them go. Governor Ashe had come out alone in his coat. He took the last name from the plate himself, halting over its vowels, and said it again to the road.

Afterward, when the frost lay thin on the plate, a small shape grew in it, closed and round, and spread into a long one, and held. It had a head. It had two arms. Illuminara, sitting on an upturned crate with her coat around her knees, did not need it translated.

**Vesh**  
We have a picture of you now. Come again when the streets knit. Come slowly.

**Illuminara**  
I will.

**Governor Ashe**  
Seventy days. My reconstruction trucks.

**Illuminara**  
Take the river road when the water drops. Longer, I know. Ilse has costed it.

Ashe let out a long breath. Then he took the pencil and, under the order to open the road, wrote the sentence that would govern it. Convoys cross only in a pulse. The marshal follows the frost. The first day is a trial. A driver who crosses outside a pulse loses his licence for a year. Beneath it he copied Sheaf's six lines out in his own hand, so that the order would carry them as terms and not as favours.

**Governor Ashe**  
And if one of my drivers decides he's in a hurry?

**Dov**  
Then he meets me at the gate, Governor. And the gate meets him first.

scenes.title: The Ninety-Third Name
paragraphs: *The line · two days before the crest, 03:49*
The first day had been the trial. At its last pulse Vesh wrote *go on*, and the warning had struck early twenty-three times since; each time Dov dropped the gate, and each time no street was cut.

On the ninth night the last bus crossed in the first pulse after the sleep quarter, a school bus with a cracked mirror and eleven people asleep across the back seats. It went over the line at fifteen kilometres an hour, and the frost did not stir.

story.title: THE ROAD THAT CUT A COUNTRY THIN AS PAPER
story.deck: The only road out of a flooding valley runs through a country as thin as paper, whose people have only ever met humans as sudden walls. Illuminara cannot perceive their plane, so she asks its speaker what a whole person would look like, and lies down across the road to show her.
story.shape: Seven scenes across eleven days: a cold line on a road, a conversation in frost, a governor's one night, a body read slice by slice, a table proved on a rolling truck and a neighbour's terms, the arithmetic of nine days, and the last crossing.

scenes.title: The Cold Line
paragraphs: *Orrin Cut, kilometre 14 · twelve days before the crest, 05:40*

The road ran through the Cut like thread through a needle, and halfway along it the air changed. Illuminara felt it before she saw the survey flags: a line of cold across the tarmac, straight as a ruled edge. Fog on the upslope side stopped at it. On the downslope side the dawn was only dawn.

Four road crew had walked into it since the autumn rains. One had lost feeling down his left side for a week. A gauge nailed to a post read minus six on the line and eleven above zero a pace either way.
Ilse Brandvold, the survey lead, had slept in her truck. She pointed at a steel plate bolted flat to the road, a metre square, white with rime.

**Ilse**  
Six weeks of geophone logs. Every ninety minutes it pulls back for about fourteen minutes, then comes down again. I thought it was groundwater. Then I put the plate on the line to measure the frost, and the frost wrote back.
Marks were forming on the rime as they watched, thin and deliberate, as if someone were breathing them there.

**Ilse**  
I have eleven hundred of those. I understand perhaps forty. The speaker is called Vesh. It's a country, Illuminara. Sheaf, it calls itself: a sheet no thicker than a coin, and the Cut goes straight through the middle of it.

**Illuminara**  
And the governor?

**Ilse**  
Opens the road at noon. Nine thousand buses and trucks, six days, no stopping. The river crests in twelve. I can't put a country on his desk. I have a steel plate and a cold spot.

Illuminara crouched and laid her palm on the rime. It burned, and under the burn she felt something she had no word for, like being looked at from the side. *I can hold a lane open,* she thought. *The lane is not the problem. I can't perceive what she can't show him, and I won't pretend to.*

scenes.title: What the Frost Said
paragraphs: *The plate on the line · twelve days before the crest, 07:10*
Vesh's words came a few strokes at a time. Ilse read them out in her flat survey voice, and Illuminara answered to the plate itself, because it seemed rude to answer to anyone else.

**Vesh**  
You are weather to us. A wall rises where there was a street, grows, narrows, is gone. Nothing is behind it. Ninety-three of us have stood inside the rising. Eleven streets are cut in two and do not rejoin.

**Illuminara**  
I'm sorry. I'm also here to ask something of you, and I would rather you heard it from me than discovered it. Nine thousand vehicles must pass in twelve days, or two hundred thousand people are under the river. I don't yet know how to pass them without cutting more of you.

**Vesh**  
You ask patience of a people whose houses you halve with every wheel. Tell me when I am allowed to be afraid.
Illuminara did not answer at once. *A reasonable question,* she thought. *A true one.*

**Illuminara**  
Now. You're allowed now. Tell me exactly what you're afraid of, so I stop guessing.

**Vesh**  
That we are not seen. A blade has no one behind it. We have never met one of you. We have met the parts of you the road lets through.

It landed in her slowly. To Sheaf a person was not a person at all. A foot was a ring that appeared, swelled and shrank. A bus was a wall. No one in that country had ever watched a thing for long enough to call it a thing.

**Illuminara**  
Show me what a wall is. Where does it start, and where does it stop?

**Vesh**  
Your road crosses us in one band, forty of your metres deep. Whatever you drive through the band is a wall in the band, as wide as the thing, for as long as it stays. If the band is full, the wall cuts a street across. In a closing the band is emptied: stalls shut, lamps out, everyone withdrawn to either side. Then a wall cuts nothing.
Ilse turned a page of her notebook and drew it as the frost wrote: a coin standing on its edge, a road through its middle, a hatched band across the road.

**Illuminara**  
So the road isn't the danger. A full band is.

**Vesh**  
Yes. And there are always some who are late.

**Illuminara**  
What would a whole one look like to you?

**Vesh**  
Slow. A shape that stays long enough to be a shape, then another a little changed. We would read it as we read a coast.
*A coast, taken one slice at a time,* she thought, and offered the only thing she had that was not a request.

**Illuminara**  
I can lie across the road and pass through the line as slowly as you choose. You set the speed. You say stop, and I stop.
The frost took a long time to answer.

**Vesh**  
It is a danger to you. It would be a danger to us if you were wrong. Come in our sleep quarter, when the streets are empty. Come with no machine.

scenes.title: One Night
paragraphs: *Staging yard, Haldane Junction · twelve days before the crest, 11:20*

Governor Halloran Ashe stood at a map of the river with a pencil behind his ear and a driver's funeral card in his breast pocket. He had buried the man on Tuesday. He heard Ilse's whole report without once looking at his watch, which Illuminara noticed and respected.

**Governor Ashe**  
I believe you. I believe there's a country in my road. I also have two hundred thousand people between a river and a hill, and a convoy that can't idle. What do you want?

**Illuminara**  
One night and the morning after. Hold the convoy here. I'm not asking you to close the road. I'm asking for a way to run it that doesn't cut anyone.

**Governor Ashe**  
That costs days. I had six. The crest is twelve.

**Illuminara**  
It may cost three. It won't cost twelve. If I can't show you something by noon tomorrow, open it. The order is yours, not mine.

**Governor Ashe**  
And if what you show me is a creature's feelings against my people's lives?

**Illuminara**  
Then I won't stand in the road. But her streets are real, Governor. So are yours.
He took the pencil from behind his ear and wrote *noon* across the staging yard on the map, hard enough to tear the paper.

scenes.title: Slice by Slice
paragraphs: *Orrin Cut, the line · eleven days before the crest, 02:20*

She lay on her back across the centre line in a thin coat, head toward Ilse's lamp, feet toward the downslope dark. Dov Karakas, the night marshal, kept the cones. Ilse knelt at the plate with a notebook on her knee. Nothing electronic was within thirty metres. Vesh had asked for that.

**Vesh**  
A thumb's width in each of your minutes. Begin.

Illuminara dug her heels into the tarmac and slid. The cold met her toes first. It crossed them like a thread drawn tight and climbed her, one band of ice laid against her skin at a time. On the plate the frost began to write, not words now but shapes, small and closed.

**Vesh**  
A ring. It grows. Another beside it. They are joining.

**Illuminara**  
My ankles. Then a leg. Then the other.

**Vesh**  
Why does it not vanish?

**Illuminara**  
Because I'm staying.

She slid on. Her knees made two long ovals, her hips one wide one, and at the ribs a curve that swelled and fell, swelled and fell. Ilse read it out in a whisper, and Illuminara felt the line of cold cross her chest like a hand laid flat.

**Vesh**  
It moves in a rhythm. Is it failing?

**Illuminara**  
Breathing. It means I'm alive.

The shape stopped changing for a long time. Illuminara lay with the cold across her ribs and her teeth beginning to chatter, and understood with a clarity that surprised her that she was being read. A country was walking the length of her, one lamp-lit street at a time, and for the first time learning that the wall had edges.
Then Vesh asked for the hand. She lifted it a thumb's width at a time, and the frost divided the curve into five, small and astonished.

**Vesh**  
You are not a blade. You are long. You have parts.

**Illuminara**  
So do you, I think.

The cold crossed her hair at 03:46. The frost drew a last round shape, and the whole of her was a drawing. At 03:49 the line melted off the plate and off the road all at once, the way a held breath is let go.

**Vesh**  
The market is closing. The streets are empty. Look.

The frost drew it for them: lanes of lamps going dark in order, doors shutting, a square emptying like a bath. Fourteen minutes of nothing. Illuminara, who had never been shown a country's evening, lay on wet tarmac and watched it breathe.

scenes.title: The Calendar
paragraphs: *The line · eleven days before the crest, 05:12*
Ilse had a sealed envelope in her breast pocket. She had written it at nine the previous evening from six weeks of geophone logs and nothing Vesh had told her, and had given it to Dov to hold.

**Ilse**  
If the logs are a calendar, it goes quiet at five-seventeen for fourteen minutes, give or take three. So eleven at the shortest. And the closing you saw at three-forty-nine was two minutes off my card. That's the part I got wrong.

**Dov**  
Two minutes is a good miss.

**Illuminara**  
Why two?
Ilse asked the plate. The frost answered quickly.

**Vesh**  
Our market runs with the river. It lags a little each cycle. Tell your surveyor to keep a table, not a constant.
Ilse wrote *table, not constant* in the margin of her envelope. At 05:18 the line melted off the road, one minute after her card. Nothing moved. Dov's thumb stayed on the radio.

**Vesh**  
Wait. Late ones are still leaving the band.
The plate stayed blank for a minute that felt like six. At 05:19 it wrote one word, small and square. *Empty.*

They sent an empty flatbed across by remote at fifteen kilometres an hour, with a second flatbed rolling up behind it. Vesh's report was on the plate before the first truck cleared the line. *No street cut. A wall passed. Nothing was in it.*

The frost came back at 05:29, a white line creeping across the tarmac from the plate outward. Ilse looked at her watch. Eleven minutes, the very bottom of her range, and the second flatbed was a length from the line, rolling on the card's promise of two more.

**Vesh**  
Market reopens. Stop.

**Dov**  
That's a red light I can read.
Dov dropped the gate. The flatbed halted a metre short of the line, and nobody argued with a strip of frost.

**Illuminara**  
And if it had been inside?

**Vesh**  
A wall through the stalls at the hour they are raised. Brass Street, fourteen stalls. We would have counted them.

Ilse wrote *eleven* under *table, not constant* and circled it twice. Illuminara watched the gate and thought of what the governor needed to hear. *Sheaf can stop us, and does, and we can see it happen.* Then she thought of the other thing, which was harder.

**Illuminara**  
Vesh, whose word would I be carrying to him? I don't want to speak for Sheaf. I want the governor to hear Sheaf.

**Vesh**  
I speak for the market, because the market is the part of us that meets your road. For the eleven cut streets I carry. I do not decide. Wait.
The plate stayed white until 09:40. Then it wrote at length, and Ilse read it aloud twice before she trusted her voice.

**Vesh**  
The streets have spoken. One: your trial may become a convoy. One lane, never the sleep quarter, never the lane over Brass Street. The first day is a trial, and if a street is cut it ends. Two: we strike a warning three of your minutes before we reopen, and we keep it even when it costs the market its early stalls. We will write you each morning the day's closings. Three: we say stop when we choose, and you do not ask why. Four: when your people have gone, the road rests seventy days while the cut streets knit. Five: if the road is ever widened, there is a seat for us, and the answer in it is ours. Six: the ninety-three go where your laws are kept, in our script.
Ilse read it back to the plate, line by line, and Vesh corrected one word.

**Vesh**  
Not a courtesy. A warning. Write warning.
She wrote it.

scenes.title: Nine Days
paragraphs: *Staging yard, Haldane Junction · eleven days before the crest, 11:50*
She put the arithmetic on the governor's table because he had asked for arithmetic and nothing else, and beside it Ilse laid the plate's transcript, Sheaf's six lines in Ilse's hand.

**Illuminara**  
Those aren't mine. Sheaf wrote them, Ilse read them back, and Vesh corrected one word. You sign them or you don't.
Ashe read the six lines slowly, the way a man reads a contract he intends to be held to.

**Governor Ashe**  
Eleven minutes. You told me fourteen last night.

**Ilse**  
Fourteen is the middle. At five-twenty-nine we watched the bottom, with a truck rolling.

**Illuminara**  
So we plan on the bottom. Eleven, less one for the band to empty and three for the warning, leaves seven to drive, at fifteen kilometres an hour. The spacing is Dov's.

**Dov**  
While we waited on the streets this morning I took the worst pair on the manifest down the approach grade: a loaded gravel tipper behind the lightest van, cold tarmac, red light dropped at fifteen. Driver's reaction counted, the tipper needed ten metres to stop. So nobody enters closer than ten metres clear of the one ahead, and the entry light holds them until they're clear. That's for a lead that vanishes. A real lead needs a few metres of its own to stop, so the margin is real.

**Illuminara**  
The manifest's mean length is ten metres, so ten clear is twenty nose to nose on average. A long vehicle waits longer, a short one less. Twelve and a half vehicles a minute, eighty-seven a pulse. Sixteen closings a day, Sheaf keeps four for sleep, twelve pulses. A thousand and forty-four a day.

**Governor Ashe**  
Nine thousand over a thousand and forty-four.

**Illuminara**  
Eight days and a bit more than half. The crest is eleven days off. Lose two pulses every day, to frost or a breakdown or a gate, and it's ten days and a third. You still clear the valley before the water.

**Governor Ashe**  
I wanted six.

**Illuminara**  
I know. Nobody is cut.
Ashe studied the table, then the frost photographs Dov had pinned beside it. For a while he said nothing.

**Governor Ashe**  
And the eleven streets already cut? I won't open a road I can be accused of lying about.

**Illuminara**  
Line four. After the evacuation the Cut closes to heavy traffic for seventy days, ambulances only, and only in a closing. They knit if nothing crosses.

**Governor Ashe**  
Seventy days. My reconstruction trucks.

**Illuminara**  
Take the river road when the water drops. Longer, I know. Ilse has costed it.

Ashe let out a long breath. Then he took the pencil and, under the order to open the road, wrote the sentence that would govern it. Convoys cross only in a pulse. The marshal follows the frost. The first day is a trial. A driver who crosses outside a pulse loses his licence for a year. Beneath it he copied Sheaf's six lines out in his own hand, so that the order would carry them as terms and not as favours.

**Governor Ashe**  
And if one of my drivers decides he's in a hurry?

**Dov**  
Then he meets me at the gate, Governor. And the gate meets him first.

paragraphs: *The line · two days before the crest, 03:49*
